# Volume 2 — XVIII An Adventure on the Tory Road

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“Nell,” declared Robin, who sat upright in his bed while resting his chin upon his hands, “Nell, where is sleep? Every night individuals go to sleep, and naturally I understand that it is the location where I accomplish the actions I dream, yet I desire to learn where it is situated and the way I travel there and return without being aware of anything . . . and wearing my nighty as well. Where is it?”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0000 }

At the west gable window, Nell knelt as she observed the evening sky, which resembled a huge blossom featuring crocus-colored petals and a center of burning yellow. Turning her head when Robin questioned her, she replied in a dreamy manner,
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0001 }

“‘Across the peaks of the moon, Through the vale of the shadow.’”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0002 }

Cedric Stanhope would have grasped what this signified, or forged a significance for it on his own, had he not known; yet pragmatic Robin, whom Nell frequently observed with despair possessed no imagination whatsoever, was merely perplexed and repulsed.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0003 }

“Nell, it is my belief that you are merely speaking absurdity.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0004 }

“Naturally, I was, my dear young man. Are you unaware that merely the most senseless people speak reasonably without exception?”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0005 }

“Well, it seems to me that a reasonable query deserves a reasonable reply,” Robin stated, sounding offended.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0006 }

“Oh, you lack the age to comprehend,” Nell remarked. Nevertheless, uttering those words made her feel somewhat humiliated; after all, had she not earnestly promised herself—with sharp memories of numerous comparable rejections suffered during her own childhood—that no child would ever hear her say they were too young to comprehend? Even so, she was now guilty of the exact same thing . . . so vast, on occasion, is the distance dividing principle from action.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0007 }

“Indeed, I am attempting to increase my height as much as I can,” Robin remarked, “yet it is a process that one cannot hasten significantly. Should Thirza prove less frugal regarding her jam, I am convinced my growth would occur much more rapidly.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0008 }

“Robin, Thirza does not lack generosity,” Nell remarked sternly. “Making a statement like that shows a great deal of ungratefulness on your part.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0009 }

“An alternative term exists with the identical definition that sounds much nicer, though it slips my mind at the moment,” Robin stated, his forehead creasing deeply. “I listened to Thirza state that she was that very thing, herself, a few days ago.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0010 }

“Should you imply thrifty, that is completely distinct from being tightfisted. Being thrifty is a wonderful quality for someone to possess. Had Thirza been tightfisted, she never would have brought in you and Lucy upon the death of your mother. Might you have preferred residing alongside Mrs. Wiggins?”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0011 }

“I certainly wouldn't!” Robin declared with great emphasis. “And going to Uncle Richard's isn't something I want either. Being here suits me much better, despite Thirza being so stingy with the jam, simply because you are with me, Nell. Tell me, Nell, could you share a tale with me before I drop off? Skip the fairy tales. Girls might like them, I guess, but my preference is for something thrilling . . . packed with slaughter and gunplay, plus a burning home, and similar captivating events.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0012 }

It was lucky for Nell that, just then, Thirza shouted from her own chamber.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0013 }

“Nell, Isolde’s signaling very fast, so you ought to check what she wants.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0014 }

Nell hurried to the east gable, where she observed bursts of light shining through the dusk from Isolde’s window in clusters of five, signifying, in line with their former childhood signals, “Come over at once for I have something important to reveal.” Placing her white shawl upon her head, Nell rushed across the Whispering Wood and through Mr. Bell’s pasture corner until she reached Pear Hill.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0015 }

“Nell, I have some good news for you,” Isolde said. “Mother and I just returned to the house from Delford, where I ran into Mary Sentner from Tranter vale inside the store belonging to Mr. Blair. According to her, the old Copp girls who live on the Tory Road own a willow-ware platter that she believes is an exact match for the one at our supper. She mentioned that they will probably part with it, since Martha Copp is famous for selling anything she possibly can; however, should they refuse, another platter exists at Wesley Keyson’s place in Tullyvale which she is certain they would sell, though she cannot guarantee it is the precise type that belongs to Aunt Lavinia.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0016 }

“I will head straight to Tullyvale the following day after it,” Nell stated with determination, “and I need you to accompany me. My mind will be so relieved, because I am required to travel to town the day after that, and in what way am I able to face your Aunt Lavinia if I lack a willow-ware platter? That would prove to be far more terrible than the occasion when I was forced to admit to leaping upon the spare room bed.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0017 }

The pair of girls chuckled about the past recollection . . . regarding which, should any among my readers be unaware and inquisitive, I am obliged to direct them toward the former narrative of Nell.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0018 }

On the following afternoon, the girls set out on their journey to hunt for platters. Tullyvale was ten miles away, and the weather did not make for a particularly enjoyable trip. Conditions were extremely hot and devoid of wind, while the road was as dusty as one would anticipate following a six-week drought.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0019 }

“Oh, how I long for a prompt rainfall,” Nell lamented. “The drought has dried up everything. My heart goes out to the miserable fields, while the trees appear to reach out with open palms, begging for water. Visiting my garden causes me pain each time I step inside. Yet, I should probably refrain from lamenting a garden while the crops of the farmers are enduring such distress. According to Mr. Pettifer, the dried-out state of his pastures leaves his unfortunate cows with barely a scrap to graze on, making him feel like he is abusing his livestock whenever he looks them in the eye.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0020 }

A tireing ride brought the girls to Tullyvale, where they veered onto the “Tory” Road . . . a secluded, verdant thoroughfare whose grassy patches amid the rutted paths testified to a dearth of traffic. For the majority of its length, it was flanked by densely growing juvenile spruces pressing toward the passage, interrupted occasionally by an opening where a rear pasture of a Tullyvale homestead reached the barrier or a stretch of tree-butts blazed with weed-of-fire and goldenrod.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0021 }

“What is the reason it is named the Tory Road?” Nell inquired.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0022 }

“Mr. Wace claims the rationale resembles naming a location a grove due to its lack of trees,” Isolde stated, “since the only residents along the road are the Copp girls and, at the far end, old Martin Bovyer, a Liberal. When the Tory government held power, they constructed the road merely to demonstrate that they were active.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0023 }

The father of Isolde belonged to the Liberal party, an aspect that caused her and Nell to refrain from talking about politics. Conservative views had consistently been held by the people at Grey Shutters.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0024 }

At last the young women arrived at the former Copp property . . . an abode possessing such extreme outdoor tidiness that it would have made even Grey Shutters look inferior in comparison. Located upon an incline, the home was of an extremely traditional style, a circumstance that had required a stone cellar to be constructed beneath a single end. A state of dazzling flawlessness was achieved by whitewashing all of the house and outbuildings, while the neat, white-paled kitchen garden displayed not a single visible weed.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0025 }

“Every blind has been drawn,” Isolde remarked with regret. “It seems to me that no one is inside.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0026 }

Events unfolded precisely in this manner. A look of confusion passed between the girls.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0027 }

“I am at a loss,” Nell stated. “Were I certain that the platter was of the correct sort, I wouldn’t care about waiting for their return. However, if it is not, going to Wesley Keyson’s later might be impossible due to the late hour.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0028 }

Isolde gazed toward a particular small, square window situated above the basement.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0029 }

“I feel sure that is the pantry window,” she said, “for this house is an exact match to Uncle Charles’ at Stonebridge, where that window belongs to their pantry. Since the shade is not drawn, climbing onto the roof of that small house would allow us to peer inside the pantry, where we might catch sight of the platter. Do you suppose doing so would cause any harm?”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0030 }

“No, I don’t think so,” Nell concluded, following careful consideration, “as we are not driven by mere inquisitiveness.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0031 }

Once this significant matter of morality had been resolved, Nell got ready to climb onto the previously mentioned “little house,” a lath-built structure featuring a pointed roof that had formerly functioned as a dwelling for ducks. The keeping of ducks had been abandoned by the Copp girls . . . “because they were such untidy birds”. . . meaning the structure had remained unused for several years, except when utilized as a place of punishment for brooding hens. Even though it had been meticulously whitewashed, it was now a bit unstable, causing Nell to feel quite uncertain while she climbed up from the higher position of a keg set atop a box.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0032 }

“It will collapse under my weight, I fear,” she remarked, cautiously setting foot upon the rooftop.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0033 }

“Rest yourself against the window frame,” Isolde suggested, and Nell proceeded to rest against it. Upon looking through the glass, she observed, to her great happiness, a piece of willow-ware porcelain, precisely like the one she was searching for, sitting upon the ledge directly behind the window. All this was visible to her prior to the disaster. Her happiness caused Nell to become unmindful of how unstable her foothold was; she rashly stopped resting against the window frame and took an excited small jump of delight . . . whereupon she dropped right through the top structure as far as her underarms within a instant, remaining suspended and entirely incapable of pulling herself out. Isolde hurried inside the duck house, where she grabbed the waist of her unlucky companion in an effort to pull her downward.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0034 }

“Ow . . . don’t,” miserable Nell screamed. “Long splinters are thrusting into my skin. Try placing an object beneath my feet . . . and I might be able to pull myself upward.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0035 }

Isolde hurriedly pulled the earlier named barrel inside, which Nell discovered was barely tall enough to offer a firm support upon which to rest her feet. Nevertheless, she remained unable to free herself.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0036 }

“If I went up there, would I be able to haul you out?” Isolde offered.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0037 }

Nell gave a hopeless shake of her head.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0038 }

“No . . . the splinters are giving me too much pain. However, if an axe is available to you, my release might be chopped out by you. Oh dear, the belief that my birth occurred under an unlucky star truly begins to take hold in me.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0039 }

Isolde looked diligently, yet she failed to discover any axe.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0040 }

“I will need to seek assistance,” she stated, walking back toward the captive.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0041 }

“No, truly, you are not going to,” Nell declared with great force. “Should you do that, word of this incident will spread all over, leaving me too embarrassed to be seen. No, our only option is to wait for the Copp girls to return and make them promise not to tell. They are going to know the location of the axe and free me. Provided I remain completely motionless, I am not in pain . . . physically speaking, that is. I am curious about the price the Copp girls put on this home. The harm I caused will have to be covered by my money, yet that would not bother me if I could just be certain they would comprehend why I peeked into their pantry window. The only thing comforting me is that the dish matches the exact type I desire, and provided Miss Copp agrees to sell it to me, I will accept everything that transpired.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0042 }

“In the event that the Copp girls fail to return prior to nightfall . . . or perhaps not until the following day, what then?” Isolde inquired.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0043 }

“In the event that they have not returned when the sun sets, I guess you will be forced to seek alternative help,” Nell stated with hesitation, “however, you must not depart until it becomes absolutely necessary. Oh dear, this situation is a terrible plight. My troubles would not bother me as much if they possessed romance, like the heroines belonging to Mrs. Varley consistently do, yet they are perpetually merely absurd. Imagine the reaction of the Copp girls as they travel into their yard and observe the head and shoulders of a girl protruding from the roof of a building on their property. Hark . . . does that sound like a wagon? No, Isolde, I think that sound is thunder.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0044 }

It was unquestionably thunder, and after she completed a hurried tour of the dwelling, Isolde came back with the news that a particularly dark cloud was climbing swiftly in the northwest.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0045 }

“It looks like a severe thunder-shower is coming,” she cried out with distress, “Oh, Nell, what are we going to do?”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0046 }

“It is necessary that we get ready for it,” Nell remarked calmly. Compared to the events that had already transpired, a thunderstorm appeared insignificant. “Driving the horse and buggy under that open shed would be a good idea. By good fortune, my parasol remains inside the buggy. Take this . . . bring my hat along with you. Thirza remarked that I was foolish for wearing my finest hat to travel to the Tory Road, and she spoke the truth, just as she invariably does.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0047 }

Isolde unfastened the pony and entered the shed, precisely when the initial large raindrops began to fall. Sitting inside, she observed the ensuing deluge, which grew so dense and intense that Nell was barely visible through the curtain of water, valiantly supporting the parasol above her uncovered head. Thunder was not particularly abundant, yet the rain poured down cheerfully for almost an hour. Now and then, Nell tilted her parasol backward to wave a supportive hand toward her companion; however, talking across such a span was entirely impossible. At last, the downpour stopped, the sun emerged, and Isolde braved the yard's puddles to cross over.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0048 }

“Were you soaked terribly?” she inquired with concern.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0049 }

“Oh, no,” Nell cheerfully replied. “The rain only beat through the laths to make my skirt a little damp, while my head and shoulders are entirely dry. Do not feel sorry for me, Isolde, since it hasn't bothered me in the slightest. I continuously reflected on the great benefit of the rain and the joy it brings to my garden, while picturing how the buds and flowers would react as the drops started falling. In my mind, I crafted an exceedingly fascinating conversation involving the sweet peas, the asters, the garden's guardian spirit, and the wild canaries inside the lilac bush. I intend to record it on paper once I arrive back home. It would be wonderful if I possessed paper and a pencil to write it right this second, as I will likely lose the finest details from my memory prior to reaching home.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0050 }

A pencil was held by Isolde the faithful, who found a piece of wrapping paper within the buggy's box. After closing her wet parasol and placing her hat upon her head, Nell laid the wrapping paper across a shingle that Isolde passed to her, drafting her garden idyl in an environment that was scarcely suited for literary composition. All the same, the outcome turned out to be rather lovely, leaving Isolde “enraptured” as Nell recited the piece to her.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0051 }

“Oh, Nell, it is delightful . . . simply delightful. You must submit it to the Canadian Woman.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0052 }

Nell gave a shake of her head.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0053 }

“Oh, no, it would not be appropriate whatsoever. You see, it lacks any plot. It is merely a sequence of whims. I enjoy composing stuff like that, though obviously nothing like it could ever be published, since editors require plots, or so Honora claims. Oh, Miss Sarah Copp is over there now. Isolde, please step over and clarify.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0054 }

Sarah Copp was a diminutive individual, dressed in worn black garments, wearing a headpiece selected not for frivolous decoration but rather for durable attributes. Upon witnessing the unusual sight in her premises, she appeared predictably astonished, yet upon listening to the account provided by Isolde, she became entirely compassionate. Hastily opening the rear entrance, she brought out the hatchet, and via several deft strikes released Nell. Experiencing some fatigue and rigidity, the second girl bent low within her enclosure and gratefully stepped out into freedom again.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0055 }

“Miss Copp,” she declared with sincerity, “you must believe that my sole intention when I glanced through the window of your pantry was to find out whether a willow-ware platter was in your possession; nothing more came to my attention, nor did I seek to observe anything further.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0056 }

“Bless you, that’s all right,” Miss Sarah pleasantly remarked. “There is no need for you to worry—no damage has been done. Thank goodness, the pantries of us Copps are kept presentable continually and we do not mind who looks inside them. Regarding that old duckhouse, its destruction pleases me, because perhaps Martha will consent to its removal now. Before this, she refused every time since she thought it could be useful eventually, forcing me to whitewash it each spring. However, attempting to reason with Martha is like arguing with a post. She traveled to town today—I took her in the carriage to the station. So, you wish to purchase my platter. Well, how much will you offer me for it?”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0057 }

“Twenty dollars,” Nell stated, though she lacked the shrewdness required to contend in business with a Copp, which was evident from her opening with her asking price.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0058 }

“I suppose I will think about it,” Miss Sarah stated guardedly. “Luckily, that plate belongs to me, otherwise I would not have the courage to dispose of it in Martha's absence. Even so, I reckon she will make a scene. I assure you that Martha controls this house. Being dominated by a different woman is becoming terribly wearying for me. Nevertheless, enter, enter. You are certainly quite exhausted and famished. As for tea, I will prepare whatever I am able to, though I caution you to anticipate merely bread, butter, and a few cowcumbers. Prior to leaving, Martha placed every piece of cake, cheese, and jam under lock and key. It is her constant practice, as she claims that I consume them excessively whenever visitors arrive.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0059 }

The girls possessed an appetite great enough to appreciate any meal, and Miss Sarah’s outstanding bread, butter, and “cowcumbers” gave them complete enjoyment. As soon as they finished eating, Miss Sarah said,
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0060 }

“I am not sure I object to disposing of the platter. However, twenty-five dollars is its value. The platter is extremely old.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0061 }

Isolde nudged Nell’s foot softly beneath the table, which signified, “Don’t agree—she’ll let it go for twenty if you hold out.” Nell, however, had no intention of risking the loss of that valuable platter. Without delay, she consented to pay twenty-five, causing Miss Sarah to appear regretful that thirty had not been her asking price.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0062 }

“Well, I suppose it can be yours. Right now, I need to raise every bit of cash I can. The truth of the matter is—” tossing her head with an air of consequence, a glowing, triumphant color touched Miss Sarah’s narrow cheeks—“I am getting married—to Luther Wallace. Two decades back, he desired to marry me. My feelings for him were quite strong, yet his circumstances were poor at the time, so father sent him away. It seems I ought not to have surrendered him so submissively, yet father intimidated me and made me fearful. On top of that, I failed to realize that men were in such short supply.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0063 }

As soon as the girls had departed in safety, with Isolde at the wheel and Nell cautiously clutching the treasured platter upon her knees, the verdant, rain-cleansed emptiness of the Tory Road echoed with waves of youthful female laughter.
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0064 }

“When I travel into town on the next day, I will entertain your Aunt Lavinia with the ‘strange eventful history’ regarding this afternoon. Our experience was somewhat difficult, yet it has come to a close. The platter is in my possession, and the dust has been settled wonderfully by that rain. Consequently, ‘all’s well that ends well.’”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0065 }

“We haven’t reached home yet,” Isolde remarked with a somewhat pessimistic tone, “and it is impossible to predict what might occur prior to our arrival. Nell, you have a penchant for experiencing adventures.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0066 }

“Experiencing adventures happens naturally for certain individuals,” stated Nell placidly. “Either a person possesses a knack for them, or they do not.”
{: #nw-v02-c18-p0067 }
